title: Our account rules: size, caps and grades
teaches: Our sizing rules as one list: shares come from the account, the risk percent and the stop, rounded down, then the smaller of that and the 40% cap, bought at one price with one stop; the setup's grade picks the risk (A+ 1% to 1.5%, A and B 0.5% to 1%, B- or lower 0.25% to 0.5%, new traders 0.25%); we trade stocks at $10 or more doing $20 million a day, never over 1% of a stock's volume; the book runs to 100% of the account, or 200% on margin only when our market reading is Green; 2x and 3x ETFs are preferred; the same stock gets 3 tries a week and 6 a month; and the account is recalculated weekly or monthly.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap (A7, or the ladder's cap in a drawdown, A8).
facts.claim: Our rule: shares are the account times the risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then the smaller of that and the position cap.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: Our rule: buy the full position at one price with one stop; never scale in or add.

facts.quote: A7. Max position 40% of the account (raised from 20-25% on 2026-11-09: "RAISE THE CAP TO 40% ACTUALLY. ESPECIALLY WITH EARLY TRIMS AT 3-5R THAT IS FINE.").
facts.claim: Our max position is 40% of the account, raised on 2026-11-09 from the old 20% to 25%.

facts.quote: A tight stop never justifies a bigger position than that: a gap can jump the stop.
facts.claim: A tight stop never earns a position above the cap, because a gap can jump the stop.

facts.quote: All positions together: up to 200% of the account in a Green market (margin, B24, F60), up to 100% otherwise; so a full book of 10 averages about 20% a position.
facts.claim: The whole book can reach 200% of the account in a Green market on margin, 100% otherwise, so ten full positions average about 20% each.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: Our stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy price; that 3% is a loss on the position, not the account.

facts.quote: Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.
facts.claim: The setup's grade sets the size: A and B normal, A+ bigger, B- or lower smaller.

facts.quote: Risk by grade: A+ 1% to 1.5%; A and B 0.5% to 1%; B- or lower 0.25% to 0.5%.
facts.claim: Risk by grade: A+ 1% to 1.5% of the account, A and B 0.5% to 1%, B- or lower 0.25% to 0.5%.

facts.quote: Grading a setup (A+, A, B, B-) is discretionary and hard to define; no fixed checklist is taught as ours.
facts.claim: Grading a setup is a judgment call; we teach no fixed checklist.

facts.quote: New traders start at 0.25% risk per trade until 50 journaled trades followed the rules, then size up.
facts.claim: New traders risk 0.25% a trade until 50 journaled trades have followed the rules.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: We trade only stocks priced $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not watched at all.

facts.quote: Margin: total long positions up to 200% of the account. Risk per trade is still a percent of the account.
facts.claim: On margin the long book can reach 200% of the account, but risk per trade is still a percent of the account.

facts.quote: Margin (up to 200%, B24) is used only in a Green market.
facts.claim: Margin is used only when our market reading is Green.

facts.quote: Leveraged ETFs are preferred; no extra rules.
facts.claim: 2x and 3x ETFs are preferred under our rules, with no extra rules for them.

facts.quote: The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
facts.claim: The same stock gets at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.

facts.quote: Recalculate the account value weekly or monthly and size every trade from it.
facts.claim: Recalculate the account value weekly or monthly and size every trade from that number.

facts.quote: Risking the same percent on every trade is also fine: pick one way and write it in the plan.
facts.claim: A flat risk percent on every trade is also fine; pick one way and write it in your plan.

facts.quote: Under 1% is normal; 1.5% is the most any grade uses (E49); 2% is the absolute ceiling.
facts.claim: Under 1% risk is normal, 1.5% is the most any grade uses, and 2% is the absolute ceiling.

facts.quote: Never raise risk past the rules after a run of winners.
facts.claim: A run of winners never raises your risk past the rules.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: Stop first, a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low; size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip.

facts.quote: A market filter decides when the account trades: the app's market reading (Green, Yellow, Orange, Red).
facts.claim: The app's market reading (Green, Yellow, Orange, Red) is our market filter.

facts.quote: A “margin account” is a type of brokerage account in which the broker-dealer lends the investor cash, using the account as collateral, to purchase securities.
facts.claim: In a margin account the broker lends you cash against the account to buy securities.

facts.quote: Margin increases investors’ purchasing power, but also exposes investors to the potential for larger losses.
facts.claim: Margin raises your buying power and your possible losses.

facts.quote: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached. The price you receive upon execution, though, could be markedly different than your stop price.
facts.claim: Once triggered, a stop is a market order and can fill far from the stop price.

facts.quote: A stock’s liquidity generally refers to how rapidly shares of a stock can be bought or sold without substantially impacting the stock price.
facts.claim: A stock's liquidity is how fast its shares can be bought or sold without moving the price much.

facts.quote: Stocks with low liquidity may be difficult to sell and may cause you to take a bigger loss if you cannot sell the shares when you want to.
facts.claim: A stock with low liquidity can be hard to sell and can hand you a bigger loss.

facts.quote: Limit orders are a particularly valuable tool for trading thinly traded securities, where even small orders have the potential to represent a high percentage of an ETF's average daily volume and, as a result, impact the prevailing market price.
facts.claim: In a thinly traded security, even a small order can be a large share of average daily volume and move the price.

facts.quote: Leveraged ETFs seek to deliver multiples of the daily performance of the index or benchmark they track.
facts.claim: A 2x or 3x ETF aims for a multiple of its index's daily move.

facts.quote: For example, a 2x leveraged S&P 500 ETF seeks to deliver twice the investment return of the S&P 500 Index. This also means that this ETF will lose 2% for every 1% loss in the index.
facts.claim: A 2x S&P 500 ETF loses 2% for every 1% the index loses.

facts.quote: To determine the correct position size from this information, the investor simply needs to divide the account risk ($500) by the trade risk ($20). This means 25 shares can be bought ($500 / $20).
facts.claim: Shares come from dividing the dollars you will risk by the risk per share: $500 over $20 is 25 shares.

facts.quote: For a general rule, some traders may risk up to 1%–2% of their account on a single trade and allocate up to 5%–10% of their portfolio in any single position.
facts.claim: Schwab's general rule: risk 1% to 2% a trade and put 5% to 10% of the portfolio in one position.

facts.quote: It’s best to start small (very small) and minimize the “tuition paid” to learn the new strategy.
facts.claim: Start very small to keep the cost of learning low.

facts.quote: You can risk more as your portfolio gets bigger, but you only risk 1% of your total portfolio on any one idea.
facts.claim: With a fixed percent, dollar risk grows with the account while the percent stays the same.

facts.quote: Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: Our market reading guides risk: Green full risk per grade, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+ setups, Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: A13's stop band is 1-3% preferred, 3.5% good, up to 5%; past 5%, wait for a tighter trigger.
facts.claim: We like the stop 1% to 3% under the buy and accept up to 5%; past 5%, we wait for a tighter trigger.

facts.quote: We buy the full size at one price with one stop: no starter piece, and we never add to a loser. Adding to a working winner on strength happens, but it is rare and a feel call, never the plan.
facts.claim: We buy the full size at one price with one stop, with no starter piece and never an add to a loser. An add to a working winner on strength is rare, a feel call, never the plan.

walkthroughs.title: Size from the stop, then cap it
steps: Stop first. Then divide your dollars at risk by the risk per share. $500 over $20 a share is 25 shares.
Round down, then check the cap. You take the smaller of that number and 40% of the account.
Even a tight stop doesn't earn more than 40% of the account. A gap can jump any stop.
And you buy it all at one price, with one stop. No starter piece, and an add is never the plan.

walkthroughs.title: The grade sets the risk
steps: First you grade the setup: A+, A, B, or B- and lower. That's judgment. There's no checklist for it.
An A+ risks 1% to 1.5% of the account. A and B, 0.5% to 1%. B- or lower, 0.25% to 0.5%.
2% is the absolute ceiling, and no grade gets there. New traders stay at 0.25% until 50 journaled trades follow the rules.
Risking the same percent on every trade is fine too. Pick one way and write it in your plan.

walkthroughs.title: What we trade, and how much of it
steps: Stocks at $10 or more, doing $20 million a day. Never own more than 1% of its average daily volume.
The whole book runs to 100% of the account. On margin in a Green market, 200%, so ten names average about 20%.
We prefer 2x and 3x ETFs, no extra rules. One stock gets 3 tries a week, 6 a month.
Recount the account weekly or monthly, and size every trade off that number.

questions.q: A setup triggers. You know your account, your risk percent, your entry and your stop. How do you get the share count?
choices: How strongly you like the setup
questions.why: Account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop. The stop is in the math on purpose. Entry minus stop is what each share loses if you're wrong. Divide your dollars at risk by it and you get the shares that lose exactly your plan. Risk $500 with a $20 stop distance and you buy 25 shares. Round down, never up. Then check it against the 40% cap and take the smaller one. If the honest stop is too far away for your risk, you pass. You don't squeeze the stop to make it fit.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, then the math. Dollars at risk over the stop distance, round down, then check the cap.

wrong.Account × risk % ÷ the share price: That's sizing off the price. Your stop isn't anywhere in it, so your loss could be anything.
wrong.Account × 40% ÷ the share price: That's the 40% cap. It's a ceiling you check after the math, not your size.
wrong.How strongly you like the setup: Liking it sets the grade, and the grade picks the risk percent. The shares still come from the stop.

questions.simple: The stop sets the count. Divide the dollars you'll risk by how far your stop sits under your entry.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5)
Investopedia (s7, f09) unreachable from this machine; the key also rests on the house fact h01

questions.q: Your best idea of the year sets up and the risk math says go big. One stock still tops out at 40% of your account.
questions.why: True. 40% is the most one stock gets, your best idea included. It's a ceiling, not a target. Size from the stop first, then take the smaller of that and the cap. You might think the stop already protects you. It doesn't always. A stock can gap right through it overnight, and then the cap is what limits the damage. If the account's in a drawdown, the cap shrinks too.
questions.lesson_line: One stock, 40% of the account at most. Your best idea included.
questions.simple: True. One stock is 40% of the account at most, however good it looks, because a gap can jump your stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A7)
a number that changed recently: the cap went from 20-25% to 40% on 2026-11-09
fixed before (owner named; range misread)

questions.q: Fill in our rule.
questions.sentence: Under our rules, the most an A+ setup risks is ___ of the account.
questions.why: 1.5%. An A+ setup risks 1% to 1.5% of the account, so 1.5% is its top. It is also the most any grade uses. 2% is the absolute ceiling, and no grade uses it. 1% is the bottom of the A+ range.
questions.lesson_line: A+ gets 1% to 1.5%. No grade uses more than 1.5%.
questions.simple: It is 1.5%, the top of the A+ range of 1% to 1.5%, and the most any grade uses.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E49, A1)
a house number the owner set and already lowered once (E49: 'a little smaller')

questions.q: The market's Green. A setup triggers, but it's a B-, not one of your cleaner ones. How much of the account do you risk?
questions.why: 0.25% to 0.5%. The grade is our read on how clean a setup is, and the grade sets the size. A and B get normal risk, 0.5% to 1%. An A+ gets sized up to 1% to 1.5%. A B- gets the smallest bet we make. In a Green market you don't have to pass on it. You just risk less, because you trust it less. Save the real size for the A+. If the market slips to Orange, I only want the A+ anyway.
questions.lesson_line: Lower grade, smaller bet. A B- gets 0.25% to 0.5%.

wrong.0.5% to 1%: That's A and B money, normal size. A B- gets sized down from there.
wrong.1% to 1.5%: That's the A+ range. You'd be making your biggest bet on your weakest setup.
wrong.Pass, it's only a B-: In a Green market you don't have to skip it. You take it small, at 0.25% to 0.5%.

questions.simple: Risk 0.25% to 0.5%. A B- is a weaker setup, so in a Green market you take it smaller, not skip it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E49, D38)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: Your stop sits just 1% under your buy, so the share math wants half the account. A stop that tight lets you go past the 40% cap.
questions.why: False. The math may want half the account, but 40% is as far as one stock goes. A stop is a trigger, not a promise. Once it's hit it turns into a market order. If the stock gaps down overnight, it fills wherever the stock opens. Your 1% stop can turn into a much bigger loss before you can do anything. So the cap does the job the stop can't. You buy 40% and accept that you're risking a bit less than planned.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop buys more shares, never a bigger cap. Gaps don't care where your stop is.
questions.simple: False. A tight stop changes your share count, never the cap, because a gap can jump right over it.

deeper.counter: A stop just under your buy makes the share math huge. But a gap can jump the stop. Once the stop price is reached, the stop becomes a market order and fills wherever it can, sometimes far below. The 40% cap limits how much one gap can cost you.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A7)
a number that changed recently (the 40% cap, 2026-11-09)

questions.q: A $35 stock sets up nicely. It clears our $10 price floor. How much does it need to trade a day before we touch it?
choices: At least 20 million shares a day
questions.why: At least $20 million a day. Price and dollar volume are the two gates, and a stock has to clear both. At $35 it's fine on price, so now you check the money moving through it. Multiply the price by the average daily volume and you've got it. Why it matters: $20 million a day means plenty of buyers and sellers. You get in and out near the price you see. A thin stock is easy to buy and hard to sell. When it breaks, nobody's there at your stop, and the loss gets bigger. We don't even watch illiquid stocks.
questions.lesson_line: $10 or more, and $20 million a day or more. Thin stocks don't make the list.

wrong.At least $2 million a day: Way too thin. That's a tenth of our floor, and it's the kind of stock you can't get out of.
wrong.At least $10 million a day: $10 is the price floor, not the volume. The volume floor is $20 million a day.
wrong.At least 20 million shares a day: We count dollars, not shares. The money moving through the stock is what gets you out.

questions.simple: At least $20 million a day, so you can get out near your stop when you need to.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, D42)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: You're brand new and just funded your account. You risk 0.25% a trade until you've journaled 50 trades that followed the rules.
questions.why: True. Brand new means 0.25% a trade. And it's 50 journaled trades that followed the rules, not 50 trades of any kind. Starting that small is on purpose. Your first trades are tuition. You'll mess up entries, stops and sizes, everyone does. At 0.25% each mistake is cheap, and you're still around to learn from it. Once you've followed the plan 50 times and written it down, you size up into the normal ranges.
questions.lesson_line: New money starts at 0.25%. Earn your size with 50 clean, journaled trades.
questions.simple: True. New traders risk 0.25% a trade until 50 journaled trades follow the rules, so the early mistakes stay cheap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C37)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: Two setups trigger today. One feels like an A+, the other more like a B. How do you decide what grade each one gets?
choices: A points checklist that adds up
By how tight the stop is
By how high the share price is
questions.why: It's a judgment call. Grading is discretionary and honestly hard to pin down, so we don't teach a checklist for it. What the grade does is simple. It sets the size. A and B are normal size, an A+ gets sized up, and a B- or lower gets sized down. Then the stop turns that risk into shares. The grade picks how much you bet, the stop picks how many shares. Grade every setup in your journal and your eye for an A+ gets sharper.
questions.lesson_line: Grading is judgment. The grade picks the risk, the stop picks the shares.

wrong.A points checklist that adds up: We don't grade by points. It's a judgment call, and pretending it's a formula fools you.
wrong.By how tight the stop is: The stop sets the share count, not the grade. A tight stop doesn't make a setup an A+.
wrong.By how high the share price is: Price only decides if a stock is tradable, $10 or more. It says nothing about how good the setup is.

questions.simple: It's your judgment, with no set checklist. The grade then decides how much you risk.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E50, D38)

questions.q: $50,000 account, risking 1%. You buy at $40 and your stop goes at $38.30, under the low of the day. How many shares?
questions.why: 294 shares. Work it through. 1% of $50,000 is $500 at risk. $40 minus $38.30 is 1.7 a share. 500 over 1.7 is 294.12, so round down to 294. Never round up, that's risking more than you planned. Then the cap. At $40, 40% of the account buys 500 shares. 294 is smaller, so 294 it is. That stop is 4.25% away. Wider than I like, but it's inside 5%, so I'll take it.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars at risk over the stop distance. Round down. Then check the cap.
questions.simple: 294 shares. $500 at risk over a 1.7 stop distance, rounded down, and that's well under the cap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)
a computed key

wrong.500 shares: That's the 40% cap used as your size. Do the risk math first. The cap only limits it.
wrong.13 shares: You divided $500 by the stop price, $38.30. Divide by the distance, $40 minus $38.30.
wrong.2,941 shares: Decimal slip. That's ten times the size, risking ten times your $500.

questions.q: $50,000 account, 1% risk. You buy at $50 and the stop is $49.50, 50 cents under. How many shares do you buy?
questions.why: 400 shares, and it's the cap that decides it. The risk math is $500 at risk over 50 cents a share. That's 1,000 shares, and at $50 that's your whole account in one stock. No way. 40% of $50,000 is $20,000, and $20,000 at $50 buys 400 shares. The smaller number wins. Yes, you're now risking less than 1%. That's fine. A stop 50 cents away can't protect you from a gap.
questions.lesson_line: Risk math, then the cap. The smaller number is your size.
questions.simple: 400 shares. The risk math wants the whole account, so the 40% cap sets the size.

deeper.trap: The trap is the tight stop. Fifty cents of risk a share makes the share math huge. A gap can jump a stop that close, and a triggered stop can fill far from its price. That's why the cap, not the stop, sets this size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)
a computed key
fixed before (the question led with 'Our 40% cap applies')

wrong.1,000 shares: That's the risk math with no cap. It's your whole account in one stock.
wrong.500 shares: That's your dollars at risk, $500, used as a share count.
wrong.4,000 shares: Decimal slip on the cap. That's four times your whole account.

questions.q: Your account is $80,000. An A setup triggers and you love it, so you go to the top of the A range. How much are you risking?
questions.why: $800. A and B setups risk 0.5% to 1%, so the top is 1%. 1% of $80,000 is $800. That's what you lose if the stop gets hit at its price. Know that number before you buy, then work the shares from your stop. Loving it gets you the top of the range. It doesn't get you A+ money. The step up to 1.5% is only for the A+.
questions.lesson_line: The grade picks the percent. The percent picks the dollars.
questions.simple: $800. The top of the A range is 1%, and 1% of $80,000 is $800.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E49)
a computed key

wrong.$400: That's 0.5%, the bottom of the A range. You said the top.
wrong.$600: That's the middle of the A range, not the top.
wrong.$8,000: Decimal slip. That's ten times the 1% you meant to risk.

questions.q: A stock you like trades about 4 million shares a day on average. What's the most shares you'd ever own of it?
questions.why: 40,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 4 million is 40,000. It's all about the exit. Own a big slice of a day's volume and your own sell order moves the price against you. On a bad day you can't get out near your stop. Stay at 1% or under and the market takes your shares without noticing. This one's a share count. The $20 million a day test is a separate check in dollars.
questions.lesson_line: Never more than 1% of a stock's daily volume. Your exit has to fit too.
questions.simple: 40,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a day's volume, so we can always get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)
a computed key
the share-volume reading of D42 still awaits the owner's confirmation (conflicts line)

wrong.400,000 shares: Decimal slip. That's ten times our limit.
wrong.4,000,000 shares: That's the whole day's volume. You'd be the market.
wrong.200,000 shares: That's one-twentieth of a day's volume. Our limit is 1%, one-hundredth.

questions.story: Account $100,000. An A+ setup, so you pick 1.5% risk. Entry $20, stop $19.70, a 1.5% stop. The risk math says $100,000 in the stock.
questions.q: How big is the position?
questions.why: $40,000. The risk math says $100,000, the whole account. The cap says 40% of $100,000, which is $40,000. The smaller number wins. You end up risking less than the 1.5% you planned, and that's fine.
questions.lesson_line: The cap binds before the grade. Size from the stop, then take the smaller number.

wrong.$100,000: That's the risk math with no cap. The whole account in one stock is one gap away from a big loss.
wrong.$1,500: That's the dollars at risk, 1.5% of $100,000, not the size of the position.
wrong.$25,000: That's the old cap, 25% of the account. We raised it to 40% on 2026-11-09.

questions.simple: The position is $40,000, because the 40% cap is smaller than the $100,000 the risk math asks for.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7, E49)
a computed key

questions.q: The market's Green and you're on margin, so your buying power just doubled. Now your 1% risk per trade is 1% of the buying power.
questions.why: False. Margin changes how much you can hold, not what one trade can lose. Your risk is still a percent of the account. On margin the whole book can reach 200% of the account, and only when our market reading is Green. Base your 1% on the buying power instead and every loss comes out twice what you planned. Margin raises your buying power and your possible losses together. So keep the risk math on the account.
questions.lesson_line: Margin changes what the book can hold, never what one trade can lose.
questions.simple: False. Your risk per trade stays a percent of the account, and margin only lets you hold more.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B24, F60)
a house number the owner set (200%)

questions.story: Your buddy shows you his next trade. It's a B- setup, nothing special. He's risking 1.5% on it, his A+ size, because he wants a big month.
questions.q: What do you tell him?
questions.why: Cut it to 0.25% to 0.5%. A B- gets the smallest size we've got. He's putting his A+ bet on a setup that hasn't earned it. Wanting a big month doesn't change the grade. The chart does. And this is how a big month turns into a drawdown: the weakest setups get the biggest bets. 1.5% is for the A+, and 2% is a ceiling no grade even uses.
questions.lesson_line: The grade picks the risk, not the mood. A B- gets 0.25% to 0.5%.

wrong.1.5% is fine, risk is risk: 1.5% is A+ money. Putting it on a B- turns our sizing upside down.
wrong.Raise it to 2%, the ceiling: 2% is the ceiling, and no grade uses it. 1.5% is the most anything gets, and only an A+.
wrong.Lower it to 1%, normal size: 1% is the top of the A and B range. A B- goes smaller, 0.25% to 0.5%.

questions.simple: Cut it to 0.25% to 0.5%. A B- gets small money, however big a month he wants.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E49, D38, A1)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: Market's Green and you trade on margin. Your account is $60,000. What's the most all your positions together can be worth?
questions.why: $120,000. In a Green market the book, everything you hold, can run to 200% of the account on margin. 200% of $60,000 is $120,000. In any other market reading it's 100%, the account itself, so $60,000. That's a limit, not a goal. You get there by holding up to 10 good names while the market's paying. Your risk on each trade is still a percent of the $60,000, not the $120,000.
questions.lesson_line: Green market: the book can reach 200% on margin. Anything else, 100%.
questions.simple: $120,000. A Green market lets the book reach 200% of the account on margin.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A7, B24, F60)
a computed key

wrong.$60,000: That's 100%, the limit when the market isn't Green. Green on margin goes to 200%.
wrong.$12,000: Decimal slip. That's 20% of the account, not 200%.
wrong.$90,000: Short of the limit. Green on margin allows 200%.

questions.q: Green market, and you're fully loaded: 200% of the account on margin, spread over 10 names. About how big is each one?
questions.why: About 20% each. 200% over 10 names is 20% apiece. That's an average, not a rule. Your best idea can go all the way to the 40% cap while the others sit smaller. Without margin the book is 100%, so ten names would average 10% each. Knowing the average helps you see when one name is getting too big for the rest of the book.
questions.lesson_line: Ten names at a 200% book average about 20% each. The 40% cap is for one.

wrong.About 10% of the account: That's 100% over 10 names, the book without margin. Green on margin is 200%.
wrong.About 40% of the account: 40% is the cap for one name. Ten of those would be twice what the book allows.
wrong.About 2% of the account: 2% is the risk ceiling, a different number. Position size is what you own, not what you can lose.

questions.simple: About 20% each, because 200% spread over 10 names is 20% a name.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A7)
a computed key

questions.story: You got stopped out of the same stock Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. Those were your first three tries on it this month. Thursday it sets up again, cleaner than all three.
questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: Pass, the weekly limit is used
Pass, and drop it for the month
Take it, the setup is cleaner now
Take it, but at half the size
questions.answer: Pass, the weekly limit is used
questions.why: Pass. One stock gets 3 tries a week and 6 a month. You've used this week's three, so a fourth waits for next week, however clean it looks. Here's the reason for the limit. Three stops in a row is the stock telling you something. Either it isn't ready, or you aren't reading it right. The limit stops one name from bleeding you while you're locked in on it. These were your first tries this month, so next week you can go again.
questions.lesson_line: Same stock: 3 tries a week, 6 a month. The fourth try waits.

wrong.Take it, the setup is cleaner now: The limit has no clean-setup exception. This week's three tries are gone.
wrong.Pass, and drop it for the month: Right to pass, wrong reason. The month allows 6 tries and you've used 3. Next week you can try again.
wrong.Take it, but at half the size: Half size is still a fourth try. The limit counts tries, not shares.

questions.simple: Pass. One stock gets 3 tries a week, and you've used all 3.

deeper.trap: The monthly limit is the quiet one. These three tries count toward the month's 6. Three more next week would use up all 6. A stock that keeps stopping you out burns through the month fast.

reasons: one cited fact only (h16)
rests on the owner's rulebook (E56)
a house number the owner set

questions.story: You find a stock with a perfect chart: a tight base and a clean pivot. It's $14 a share and trades about $8 million a day.
questions.q: Can you take it?
choices: No, $14 is too low a price
Yes, if you use a limit order
questions.why: No. It passes on price, $14 is over our $10 floor. It fails on volume, $8 million a day against our $20 million. It has to clear both, and a perfect chart doesn't fix that. The danger is the exit. In a thin stock your own sell can be a big chunk of the day's trading. On a bad day there's nobody there to take your shares at your stop. I'd rather miss it. There are always liquid names setting up.
questions.lesson_line: Both tests, every time: $10 or more, and $20 million a day or more.

wrong.Yes, the price clears $10: Price is only one test. Volume is the other, and $8 million a day fails it.
wrong.Yes, if you use a limit order: A limit order helps you get filled in a thin stock. It doesn't put a thin stock on our list.
wrong.No, $14 is too low a price: Wrong reason. $14 clears our $10 floor. The problem is $8 million a day, under our $20 million.

questions.simple: No. It trades $8 million a day and we need at least $20 million, so it's off the list.

deeper.counter: Dollar volume is the test that protects your exit. In a thin stock even a small order can be a big share of the day's trading and move the price. A full position here could be hard to sell when you need out, and that hands you a bigger loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, D42)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: Semis are setting up and you want SOXL, the 3x semiconductor ETF. Levered funds like that are off limits for us.
questions.why: False. We actually prefer 2x and 3x ETFs, and there are no extra rules for them. Just know what you're holding. A levered fund aims for a multiple of its index's daily move, so it drops faster too. A 2x fund loses 2% for every 1% the index loses. A 3x moves faster still. So you size it like anything else: stop first, then the same share math. The bigger swings show up in your stop distance, and the math takes care of the rest.
questions.lesson_line: 2x and 3x ETFs are welcome here. Stop first, then the same share math.
questions.simple: False. We prefer 2x and 3x ETFs, and you size them like any stock, stop first.

deeper.trap: Preferred doesn't mean sized up. A 2x fund aims for twice its index's daily move, so it loses 2% for every 1% the index loses. The same share math still applies: the stop distance sets the shares, and your risk percent stays the same.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E54), which sits beside the SEC's daily-reset warnings (conflicts line)

questions.q: You bought a breakout this morning. Your stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, not exactly on it.
questions.why: True. A few cents under the low, not on it. The low of the day, the LOD, is where buyers stepped in today. If price breaks it, the setup's wrong and you want out. Park the stop right on the low and one quick tag can shake you out of a good trade. A few cents under means the low has to actually break. Sometimes the prior day's low is the better spot. Either way, set the stop first, and the size comes from it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the LOD or the prior day's low. Then size from it.
questions.simple: True. The stop goes a few cents under the low, so the low has to really break before you're out.

deeper.trap: If the low is far under your buy, the honest stop is wide. You don't fix that by pulling the stop up onto the low or above it. The share math gives you fewer shares, or you pass and wait for a tighter entry.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)
re-aimed off A13 so q21 no longer gives away q22's key

questions.q: You'll hear me say "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%." 3% of what?
questions.why: The position. My stop sits within about 3% of where I buy. If it's hit, I lose about 3% on that stock, not on the account. The account's loss is your risk percent, 0.25% to 1.5% depending on the grade, with 2% as the ceiling. The share count connects the two numbers. I like the stop 1% to 3% away, and I'll accept up to 5%. Past that, I wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: 3% is the stop on the stock. The account's loss is your risk percent.

wrong.The account's total value: 3% of the account on every trade would blow through our 2% ceiling. It's the stop on the stock.
wrong.Your margin buying power: Margin changes what you can hold, not where the stop sits. The 3% is on the stock you bought.
wrong.All your positions together: That's the whole book, up to 100% or 200% of the account. The 3% is one position's loss.

questions.simple: 3% of the position. The stop sits close to the buy, and the account only loses your risk percent.

deeper.trap: Read 3% as account risk and every trade sits above our 2% ceiling. Read it as the stop's width on one stock, from your buy to your stop. The account's loss is the risk percent you picked by grade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A13, E49, A1)
a house number taught as a guideline

questions.story: You set your sizes in January off a $50,000 account. It's June now. The account's up to $62,000 and you're still sizing off $50,000.
questions.q: What should you be doing?
questions.why: Recalculate weekly or monthly, either one, and size every trade from that number. Five months on $50,000 means every trade is sized for an account you don't have. With a fixed percent, your dollar risk should grow as the account grows. It cuts both ways too. Here you're only too small. If the account had dropped instead, you'd be risking more than your percent on every trade, right when you're struggling. Pick a day, update the number, size from it.
questions.lesson_line: Size from the account you have, updated weekly or monthly.

wrong.Keep $50,000, it's conservative: Sizing small is fine as a choice. Doing it by accident off an old number isn't.
wrong.Recalculate only after a drawdown: The account moves both ways. We update on a schedule, weekly or monthly, not after a hit.
wrong.Recalculate only at year end: Too seldom. Weekly or monthly, so your number is never months out of date.

questions.simple: Update your account number weekly or monthly, so every trade is sized off what you really have.

deeper.trap: Here the account grew, so the old number only made you too small. If the account had fallen, the old, higher number would risk more than your percent on every trade. Updating it keeps the percent honest both ways.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D43)
a house schedule the owner set

questions.story: An A setup triggers. Your plan says 400 shares. You're thinking 200 now and the other 200 once it starts working.
questions.q: How do you put it on?
choices: Buy all 400 now with one stop
Add the rest once it starts paying
Buy 200 now, 200 on a dip lower
questions.answer: Buy all 400 now with one stop
questions.why: All 400 at one price, with one stop. That's how we do it: full size on the trigger, no starter, and no plan to add later. The 400 already came from your stop and the cap, so it's the right risk. Split it and only half your size gets the best entry you'll see. The add comes higher with the same stop, so those shares carry more risk each. If 400 feels like too much, that's telling you something. Buy fewer from the start, or pass.
questions.lesson_line: Full size at one price with one stop. No starter, no planned adds.

wrong.Add the rest once it starts paying: That's a starter-then-add plan, and it isn't ours. Full size on the trigger, one stop.
wrong.Buy 200 now, 200 on a dip lower: If it dips, it's going against you. Adding there doubles down under the same stop.
wrong.Buy all 400 with two stops: One trade, one stop. Two stops turn one plan into two.

questions.simple: Buy all 400 at one price with one stop. We don't scale in, and an add is never the plan.

deeper.trap: Buying more on a dip feels like a better price. It's really adding to a trade that's going against you, under the same stop. If the full size is too big for the stop, buy fewer shares from the start.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A3)
fixed before (owner named in a wrong-note)

questions.story: Five winners in a row and you're feeling sharp. The market reading is Green. Your next setup is a B, and you want to put 2% on it.
questions.q: What can you risk?
questions.why: 0.5% to 1%. A B is normal size, same as it was before the streak. The streak doesn't change the setup, and the setup sets the risk. This exact moment is what the rule is for. After five winners you feel like you can't miss, so you bet big on an average setup. That's how one loser gives back a week of work. Keep the B at B size. If the next one's an A+, size up then.
questions.lesson_line: Winners don't raise the risk. The grade does, and a B is 0.5% to 1%.

wrong.2%, the ceiling: 2% is the ceiling, and no grade uses it. A B sits at 0.5% to 1%.
wrong.1.5%, the streak earned it: 1.5% is the top of the A+ range. A streak doesn't turn a B into an A+.
wrong.0.25% to 0.5%, play it safe: That's B- money. A B is normal size, 0.5% to 1%.

questions.simple: 0.5% to 1%. A B gets normal size, and a hot streak never raises it.

deeper.trap: A streak feels like proof you're sharp, and that's the moment this rule is written for. Five wins in a row don't change a B grade, and the grade sets the risk.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E49, D45, A1)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: Four traders tell you how they run their accounts. Which one is breaking our rules?
choices: A 40% position on a tight stop
questions.why: The one who's 200% long in Yellow. Margin up to 200% is for a Green market only. Yellow means you go smaller and fewer, and the book stays at 100% at most. The other three are fine. 40% is the cap, and a position can reach it. Risking the same 0.5% on every trade is allowed, just write it in your plan. 1.5% is the top of the A+ range. Margin in a shaky market is where accounts get hurt, because the losses come bigger too.
questions.lesson_line: Margin to 200% only when it's Green. Any other reading, the book stays at 100%.

wrong.A 40% position on a tight stop: That's fine. 40% is the cap, and you're allowed to reach it. Going over it breaks the rule.
wrong.Flat 0.5% risk on every trade: Same percent every trade is fine with us. Pick one way and write it in your plan.
wrong.1.5% risk on every A+ setup: That's the top of the A+ range. Inside the rules.

questions.simple: The 200% book in Yellow. Margin to 200% is only for a Green market.

deeper.trap: A 200% book sounds bold, and in a Green market it's ours to use. The market reading decides it. In Yellow, Orange or Red, the book stays at 100% of the account.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A2, A7, B24, E49, F60)
